BiHeat

two matrices in one heatmap

Diagonally split heatmap cells: the upper triangle encodes one matrix, the lower triangle encodes the other.

BiHeat draws two matrices of the same shape in a single heatmap by cutting every cell along a diagonal. One value goes in the upper triangle, the other in the lower, built on ggplot2. The comparison lives inside one cell, at the resolution of a single row and column, so the eye stays in one place.

Neighbours worth knowing: corrplot has corrplot.mixed(), which draws one display above the matrix diagonal and another below it, for correlation matrices. ComplexHeatmap reaches a split cell through a custom cell_fun, alongside its clustering and annotation machinery. BiHeat splits each individual cell, gives each half its own gradient, and takes two plain matrices.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gcol33/BiHeat")

Quick start 

library(BiHeat)

set.seed(1)
species   <- LETTERS[1:6]
sites     <- letters[1:8]
observed  <- matrix(runif(48), 6, 8, dimnames = list(species, sites))
predicted <- observed + matrix(rnorm(48, sd = 0.1), 6, 8,
                               dimnames = list(species, sites))

biheat(observed, predicted)

Upper triangle is observed (white to red), lower triangle is predicted (white to blue). Where the two disagree, the split is visible.

Two matrices of the same shape come up constantly: observed vs. predicted, mean vs. variance, correlation vs. significance, train vs. test, model A vs. model B, before vs. after. All of them fit one BiHeat plot.

One call or three stages

biheat() is the one-shot entry point. It is exactly equivalent to the three-stage lifecycle below, so use whichever reads better in context:

# one-shot
biheat(observed, predicted, scale = "shared", split = "up")

# lifecycle
breed(observed, predicted) |>
  incubate(scale = "shared", split = "up") |>
  plot()

breed() pairs the two matrices into a clutch and aligns them on overlapping row and column names, then computes Pearson and Spearman correlation, RMSE, MAE, and NA counts. incubate() layers on rendering options (additive, the way ggplot2’s + is). plot() draws.

clutch <- breed(observed, predicted)
clutch
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: observed (6 x 8)
#>   lower: predicted (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.955   rmse: 0.0908   mae: 0.0693

Public API

Function Role
biheat() One-shot heatmap from two matrices
breed() Pair matrices into a clutch (auto-aligns names)
incubate() Set rendering options on a clutch (additive)
plot(clutch) Render a clutch, panel and paired legend
switch_sides() Swap which matrix is upper / lower
straighten() Flip the diagonal direction
bothways() Toggle separate / shared colour scales
comes_out() Pull the tidy data back out
geom_biheat() Draw split cells as a ggplot2 layer
bi_legend() Paired-palette legend as a standalone grob
palettes() Bundle paired gradient palettes
theme_biheat() Minimal heatmap theme

The verbs go clutch-in, clutch-out, so they chain:

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  switch_sides() |>   # swap which matrix is on top
  straighten() |>     # flip the diagonal
  bothways() |>       # toggle separate <-> shared scale
  plot()

Separate or shared scales

  • scale = "separate" (default) gives the upper and lower triangles their own numeric ranges. Use it when the two matrices measure different things (correlation vs. p-value, mean vs. variance).
  • scale = "shared" puts both triangles on a common range, so cross-triangle comparisons are meaningful. Use it when the matrices are directly comparable (observed vs. predicted in the same units, model A vs. model B accuracy).

Inside a ggplot

geom_biheat() draws the same split cells as a layer, from a long data frame with one row per cell. Each triangle carries its own gradient, so the fill scale stays free for the rest of the plot.

library(ggplot2)

cells <- comes_out(breed(observed, predicted))

ggplot(cells, aes(col, row, upper = upper, lower = lower)) +
  geom_biheat() +
  theme_biheat()

comes_out() returns one row per cell, which is the shape the layer wants. Neither triangle consumes the fill scale, so it stays free for another layer, and facets, coordinate systems, and themes all work as usual.

bi_legend() returns the paired-palette key as a standalone grob for figures where the panel is assembled separately.
